speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say how pleased I am to see that the Progressive Conservative opposition has decided to raise today such an important matter as energy. It is a matter which, of course, is of concern to all Canadians, and I hope that in the few hours the members of the House will spend on that matter they will have the opportunity to deal with the options open to us.
Energy

I must say I regret the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) has left the House. I was inclined to be a little bit harsh on him until I noticed that he does not have the responsibility for energy issues in his party and that the spokesman for the Conservative party on energy is absent from the House. There were so many distortions and a lack of knowledge of the real situation in the energy field in the speech of the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre that one would be very tempted to take to pieces the statement he put before the House. In fact I was rather surprised at the tone of the motion put before the House.
When I heard that the Conservatives wanted to debate energy today, somehow I expected the hon. member would relate it to Thanksgiving that took place yesterday and subconsciously he might be giving thanks that the energy policy of this country is under the direction of a government which has established national goals that will best serve the interests of every Canadian.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext: If one looks at the record of the Conservative party when it was in office last year, indeed its failure can be attributed to its failure to come to grips with the essential energy issues our policy is addressing. I do not want to spend much time on this, but if one looks at the sad record of the Conservative party during its eight months in office, one wonders how they can even raise the energy issue in the House. What does Mr. Speaker remember of their so-called policies on energy?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext: Sweet nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext:
Well, a few things. First there was their attempt to destroy Petro-Canada. That was the first thing they put forward.
Then they allowed the oil stocks in this country to deplete to such a degree that in November and December of last year they were required to set up the Emergency Supply Allocations Board because we were concerned that there would not be enough heating oil to take us through the winter. That was the second element of the so-called energy policy of the Conservative party.
The third element was that they severely damaged our relations with our suppliers. Indeed there was concern as to what would happen over the next while in terms of our supplies from abroad. I do not have to spend much time talking about what that government did to our relationship with Arab countries with their famous Canadian embassy-in-Israel debacle. But the fact is that they seriously jeopardized our relations with all Arab countries and neglected to develop relationships that should have been kept very warm with the government of Mexico, a potential supplier.
Then there was the cherry on the cake, as we say in French, la cerise sur le gateau. They came with their famous budget in

October 14, 1980
Energy
which they imposed savage taxation on Canadians with large price increases which fortunately both opposition parties at the time, ourselves and the New Democratic Party, rejected categorically.
Since they have been in opposition the Conservatives have continued very much the negative stance they adopted vis-a-vis energy, as was evident this afternoon during the course of the speech of the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre. What have we heard in the last few months? There has been the kind of haranguing we witnessed this afternoon during question period and during the speech of the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre, and the doom and gloom worries and predictions of members of the Conservative party. 1 could add to this their self-induced paranoia about the possible gas export tax. They do not even realize the electricity of this country has been taxed for something like 35 years between 1928 and 1963 and that we have had an export tax on oil in this country since 1974.
In effect, apart from calling for higher and higher prices and toeing the line of the fat cats with company-paid cars and expense accounts, the Conservative party has contributed- indeed, as one of my colleagues so ably said, "sweet nothing"-to the development of energy policy in this country. I do not want to spend much time on the demise of the opposition. I would like to talk about our record, our plans, what we have done and what we plan to do.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext: That will be a shorter speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext:
1 could take a lot of time, contrary to what the hon. member opposite has been saying. What we have done between 1974 and 1979 and what we intend to do over the next few years is to continue the policy of moderate price increases that will allow the industry to prosper, that will allow the producing provinces to see their revenues and wealth increasing but will also protect the consumer in this country and prevent inflation from running away in Canada. This policy which we have had in effect over the last few years has proven effective and, as it is even now, this year.
Everyone knows that in the fifties and sixties Canada's inflation rate was higher than in the United States. What we see this year, in good part, is that our energy prices are indeed lower than in the United States. The inflation rate in the United States at the present time is running at well over 12 per cent-12.8 per cent in August, 1980-while the rate in Canada was 10.7 per cent at that time. This is significant in terms of the Canadian standard of living as compared to the American standard of living.
What are our objectives? We have three objectives which we stated quite clearly before the Canadian public during the election and since-only the Conservatives have not heard them yet. The first one differentiates us from the Conservatives. I heard the hon. member saying supply was at the core of their policy. Supply is their obsession and, as a result, the only thing they can think of is giving more money to the companies,
as if this would necessarily produce one more barrel of oil tomorrow. In effect, it has been proven that this was not necessarily the case. Even if you were to double the price of oil tomorrow there would not be more activity taking place in this country because, as hon. members well know, the industry has been occupied at full capacity over the last few years.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext:
The objective in this country should be to achieve energy security, which includes looking after supply. It also includes, just as much, looking after substitution, the development and encouragement of Canadians to go into other sources of energy rather than oil, of which we have an abundance. Second, is conservation. We should encourage Canadians to use energy in a much wiser way than we have done in the past. That is our first objective-energy security.
Our second objective is fairness, which means fairness between regions, between producers and consumers, and between levels of government.
Our third objective is to provide Canadians with an opportunity to participate in that industry which will make them not only employees but full partners in the oil and gas industry. These are our objectives.
We have already taken steps in those directions over the last few months, since we have been in office. The first step has been to save Canadian consumers from the infamous 18-cent tax the Conservatives wanted to impose upon Canadians in their budget of last December, a measure which would have cost the Canadian consumers this year over $2 billion more than they have had to pay since we took office.
Our second step has been to improve and increase the security of supply in Canada. We have re-established our traditionally good relationships with the OPEC countries and the other oil producing countries which are not members of OPEC.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext: What about Iran and Iraq?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext: These steps have taken place over the last few months and we have succeeded in re-establishing those relationships which had been either destroyed or jeopardized by the stupidity of indifference of the previous Conservative government. And today, in spite of the Iran-Iraq conflict, Canada is probably the country in the world with the best balanced sources of supply with regard to its oil supply.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext: You didn't have anything to do with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext: We have not only relied upon our contacts with other countries in the world producing oil, we have acted inside Canada. One of our first steps was to encourage intensified activities in the Canadian oil and gas industry. In the last few months drilling in western Canada has gone up in comparison with last year.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext:
That was planned years ago.
October 14, 1980

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext: This year we estimate 8,300 wells will be drilled in western Canada compared with 7,400 last year. The hon. member may talk as much as he wants; the fact is they are there, and I invite him to look at them. If you look at Canada's offshore activities, there were nine wells drilled last year, and 19 this year. This is a clear indication of what has happened inside Canada in the oil and gas industry in the last year.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext: What about the tar sands?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext:
I am getting to the tar sands in a moment and I will have more to say about this than you will like.
In addition to encouraging oil and gas activities in Canada, we have given our full endorsement to Petro-Canada, an endorsement that had been sorely lacking under the Tories, and in effect we have reinstated to Petro-Canada the $80 million the Conservatives had cut off from that company. That company is now one of the most active and dynamic companies operating in the oil and gas industry in Canada, with the full support of the government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION

speechtext: I suspect the hon. member from Calgary is going to die from apoplexy and, if you could do something about him, Mr. Speaker, that would be quite helpful.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION

speechtext: I thought it was a case of apoplexy, but I regret to say it is only a case of lack of elementary courtesy. There is not much I can do about his lack of education.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext: Courtesy requires honesty in the House, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext:
As far as the activities of this government are concerned, I have indicated that we have fully supported Petro-Canada and we intend to continue to increase that support. We have also indicated a full program for upgrading our refineries. The net result of the upgrading of the five Canadian refineries will mean that something in the order of 125,000 barrels a day of residual oil will be much better used in this country in the next few years. In this way we will be able to reduce our dependence on imported oil.
Finally, we put before the producing provinces last July a fair and generous offer. That offer meant that the western provinces would have obtained over the next four years something like $40 billion. And even more recently we decided to increase our offer further to $38 a barrel for tar sands and heavy oil, plus indexation of that price to the cost of living over the next few years, plus the possibility of reopening this agreement after five years of operation if for any reason it was found that this price was inadequate.
Energy
This, indeed, was a most generous offer, and it certainly answered the expectations of the proponents of the various tar sands and heavy oil plants. As a matter of fact, I can state in this House that this offer corresponded exactly to the request made to us by the proponents of the Cold Lake plant. So, let us not hear stories and arguments from the other side that the federal government is not co-operating with regard to tar sands and heavy oil development. Let us not hear stories that the federal government is delaying the implementation of those projects.
If there is any delay, it is not the fault of the federal government and it is not the fault of the proponents of those various projects. I leave it to the opposition to reach its own conclusion on whose fault it is if there is any delay at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I indicated that our policy is first of all to ensure the security of supplies for Canadians, whether it be in the form of supplies from abroad or in the form of increased production within Canada. And I indicated we have already taken a number of steps in Canada to reach that objective, whether it be in the form of the massive support we gave Petro-Canada, the support we gave business to make sure the oil industry would fully develop under our leadership, or yet the extremely reasonable and adequate prices we offered the producing provinces to reach an agreement regarding the production of oil and gas in this country. But it is a matter not only of increasing production, but also of encouraging Canadians to change their habits as consumers and be less dependent on oil than they have been in the past by encouraging them to use other forms of energy.
Just a few months after taking over my department I announced a national objective for this decade which should enable us to arrive at a situation where only 10 per cent of the residential, commercial and industrial sectors would use oil which means that 90 per cent of those sectors would depend on natural gas, electricity or other forms of energy for their supplies.
In fact, if we could reach that objective-and there is no doubt in my mind we can-we could reduce tomorrow morning our oil consumption by 375,000 barrels a day which would be about the equivalent of our total current imports and the equivalent of the construction of three tar sands plants like Syncrude. That objective is fundamental to our policy, and we firmly intend to reach it. Indeed, we have again already taken steps in that direction. We have already announced the approval of the construction of the pipeline east of Montreal and for Quebec, and we have indicated we were also encouraging the extension of that pipeline to the maritime provinces as soon as possible.
I recently announced an additional program for the solar energy industry in order to help it achieve state-of-the-art

October 14, 1980
Energy
technology in this area, through federal subsidies and a very generous tax system.
I recently signed a new agreement with Saskatchewan and Manitoba as well as with the Yukon and the Northwest Territories concerning energy conservation and alternate forms of energy. These are some of the measures we have taken. It is our intention not only to encourage Canadians to substitute other forms of energy for oil consumption but also to encourage them, by all means available, to conserve energy even more.
For example we have allocated more than $200 million this year to the EnerSave Program, to encourage Canadians to insulate their homes much more efficiently than we have done in the past. We already signed some contracts to promote better insulation in federal buildings throughout Canada. We have launched a public education campaign whose significance the Progressive Conservatives are deriding, but that is most important to reach that objective. If I had a parallel to make, it would be with the policy followed by the Canadian government around 1974 or 1975, the new perspective on the health of Canadians, a policy that succeeded not only in Canada but also in other countries, a policy that has been internationally recognized as a breakthrough in government health policy. What we intend to do in the energy sector is something similar. What does this mean? It means relying on citizens, recognizing that citizens themselves, when given a sense of direction by government policy, can change their lifestyles and readily co-operate to reach clear and well-defined objectives that are both in their own interest and the interest of the country as a whole. That basic direction is the one this government intends to follow, even if it does not please the opposition, by calling upon each Canadian citizen to do his share to ensure that Canada will become truly and completely self-reliant in energy matters over this decade.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, whether it is the question of increasing energy security through increasing supply, better conservation, or substitution of other forms of energy, all three approaches are fundamental to an energy policy for this country. These are the basis for our approach to the question on oil and gas. In a few weeks the federal government will release a national energy program which will supplement all the steps that we have already taken in the last few months and that the Liberal governments have taken since 1974.
What we will not do is follow the actions of the previous Conservative government which established a budget with all kinds of oil and gas increases, but without any program to ensure energy security for Canadians. What we will do is implement our objectives and commitments to the Canadian public concerning security, fairness, and an opportunity to participate.

speechtext: What about price?

speechtext: With regard to energy security, we will stop Canadian dependence on imported oil well within this decade.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

speechtext: With regard to fairness, first of all we will put a price on oil in Canada which will be related to Canadian cost of production and which will not depend on the gyrations of the international cartel, OPEC.

speechtext: Yes, it will be a "made-in-Canada" price based on the Canadian cost of production.

speechtext: Is that the same one you talked about a year ago?

speechtext:
In fairness, we will also introduce a better and more fair division of revenues between the federal government and the governments of the oil producing provinces.

I should like to put on record what the situation is in other federal states where the resources are owned by the component states or provinces. In Texas, for instance, a federal state just south of here, the situation-

speechtext: Oh, oh!

minister must be aware that there is something important going on in Toronto today.

speechtext:
For the moment, I am not putting a question to the minister. I am beginning my comments. This disturbs the hon. member. I can excuse the absence of the minister convinced as I am that he has important responsibilities. Mr. Speaker, I heard similar comments some ten years ago and this government which was then in power had begun to speak about energy self-sufficiency. I do not forget the practical wish expressed by the minister to the effect that Canada should be autonomous in energy matters. We entirely agree about that, the difference being the means to be used. There is no doubt about it. We had considered and suggested some steps aimed at energy self-sufficiency in the interests of Canadians. Nobody can prevent us from repeating it. This was still clear a few months ago.
However, what happened in the past ten years? This is why we can condemn the government for failing to practise several years ago what they are now preaching. This is not a new problem, Mr. Speaker. The minister mentioned 1974 to 1979. I remember that in 1978 and 1979, for merely partisan reasons, this government deferred general elections on three occasions, thus delaying the implementation of essential steps which are still required to get close to world prices.
I think present members of this House or those who sat from 1974 to 1979 will remember perfectly well that there was a period of eighteen months over which the election was deferred three times before being held in 1979, and the Minister of Finance refused to apply certain increases that were necessary to meet the budgetary requirement for energy self-sufficiency.
I believe we must remind Canadians that that was the sinister doing of the government that is still leading the country at this time. So when the minister talks about his efforts, his proposals, the importance of self-reliance for Canada and less dependency upon foreign countries, there is a ten-year lapse the government must live with and be blamed for and that is what we are going to do. We must recall we have an urgent need of a policy that will enable us to reach and maintain self-reliance.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to talk more particularly about my province. A few moments ago, an hon. member talked
about Ontario. Others will also take the floor. So I would like to tell you for a few minutes about modern Quebec. In order to do that, one has to acknowledge the clearly economic character of its evolution. It is true that cultural and linguistic considerations have stimulated modern Quebeckers in their efforts and that that has caused an acceleration in the evolution of Quebec in the sixties. But let us not allow the acknowledgement of the French fact in Canada to blind us and make us forget about the economic problems which are at the root of the Quebec quiet revolution.
The Quebeckers of today and especially the workers aged between 34 and 45 have benefited from a period of growth in North America which gave them a lifestyle their parents had never enjoyed. The universality of education and television placed them before an opened window on the world and consequently, like it or not, they are fully aware of the values currently defended in our times.
Mr. Pierre Laurin, Director of Hautes Etudes Commer-ciales, this dynamic Quebecker who embodies so well the virtues of this generation 1 am talking about, reminds us of this often and proudly. The Quebec entrepreneur, and here I also include our outstanding Quebec women who so successfully harmonize the qualities of the heart and of the mind, the Quebec entrepreneur emerged during the last two decades. Whether a technocrat, an industrialist or owner of a small business already dealing in exportations, or a leader in our labour unions, this entrepreneur, and here I use the word in its largest definition, is much more concerned with the present and the future of Quebec than his grandfather was concerned with its past. Quebeckers today are living intensely in the present and are looking forward with great energy to the future. They can afford to do so because they have had the wisdom to weigh the respective merits of a cherished past, a present they want to enjoy fully, and a future they would like promising and secure.
And now, Mr. Speaker, if you will allow me, I would like to get to the heart of the matter we are discussing today, that is energy as a resource, since up until now I have spoken of the creative energy of Quebeckers.
Energy has been the key that opened the door to modern day Quebec just as its abundant production lead to the industrialization of the province in the nineteenth century. We all recall that the creation of Hydro-Quebec represented an important phase in the evolution of Quebec. The majestic and powerful rivers of Quebec prove beyond the shadow of a doubt that God smiles favourably on my native province. The fact that Quebeckers recognized the economic potential of these rivers also fills me with pride. Manic, that gigantic power station which provides energy to Quebec, was created by French-speaking engineers, technicians and workers, which disproved once and for all the shameful misconception about the ability of Quebeckers.
October 14, 1980

Nobody today can claim that French-speaking Quebeckers are strangers to science, entrepreneurship, and leadership in the business community, the big guys in other words! There is no doubt today that French-speaking Canadians are just as competent in the marketplace as in the realm of ideas. And as if this were not enough luck in itself, natural energy resources ensure the present economic viability of Quebec as well as its future self-sufficiency. For the hydro power of Quebec, the potential of its gas and uranium reserves, the latter giving an indication of its future nuclear capability, the studies on alternate sources such as solar energy of the treatment of waste materials along with the use of a growing technology oriented manpower, all these elements hold in store a definite energy-oriented future for Quebec.
Unfortunately, just as its purely economic future had been jeopardized by the narrow conceptions of a number of previous administrations which, due to a spirit of adventure or by sheer neglect, had gone astray from the natural evolutionary trend of Quebec, this energy future is now in compromised. The federal Liberal government, by appealing to the needs of Quebeckers for economic security during the referendum campaign got a reprieve or, as people said, the last chance for federalism. Those same Liberals have now forsaken them. The lack of courage and honesty of the federal Liberals, their neglect with regard to their economic and energetic fate are quite scandalous, Mr. Speaker. It is indeed true that Quebeckers would rather have a constitution that is really theirs, home made in Canada and reflecting their pride. But just as they rejected the hang-ups of previous administrations which no longer cared about their real needs, or rather about their real needs as a whole, both those of the heart and of the body, Quebeckers should reject the narrow views of the present federal administration. To those who claim that man does not live by bread alone, I would simply answer that they probably always had all the bread they needed and can afford to make such a selfish comment.
The economic future of Quebec will ensure the cultural and linguistic future of Quebec, it is as simple as that. They are interrelated, and Quebeckers know it. This is why so many of them are thinking of getting hold of the economic levers to achieve their aims. This is why so many demagogues play also with the feelings of Quebeckers when it suits them while others play with their fear in economic terms. Sometimes, some people succeed in persuading Quebeckers to put their needs in terms of economic security and growth in the background and to follow their hearts. But Quebeckers pull themselves together eventually. This time, however, I am afraid that they do not have enough time to do so.
Without a secure energy supply, Quebec will miss the boat. Besides, energy is the greatest challenge Canada has ever faced as well as the main factor in its future economic development. In terms of energy, Canada is behaving now as
Energy
an underdeveloped country, while it should prepare for the most glorious times in its history.
Our dependency on foreign oil imports is increasing instead of decreasing contrary to what the federal Liberal ministers generally, and especially the minister concerned, would have us believe. Quebec is dependent on foreign oil by as much as 60 per cent. Quebeckers know what is going on now in Iran, Mr. Speaker. Like all other Canadians, they can watch it on television. But are Quebeckers aware that not so long ago, Nova Scotia, Quebec's neighbouring province, was fully dependent on Iran for its oil supplies? And I am not talking here about the requirements of corporations or faceless groups, but what Canadians need to heat their homes and fill up their gas tanks.
Canada is importing oil from abroad, from Venezuela, Mexico and Saudi Arabia. It is in the latter area that Iran and Iraq are fighting their war. These supplies of fuel oil and gasoline are not intended for western Canada or even Ontario for the most part, but for Quebec and the maritimes. Should there be another war, another revolution, like in Iran, or even a natural plague like an earthquake, where would Quebec find its oil? Today Quebec depends heavily on oil for its heating, automobiles and industry.

I am used, Mr. Speaker, to hearing certain comments from the other side but they are also invited to express their concern about the absence today of guarantees of self-sufficiency in the area of energy. Quebec depends on oil for 75 per cent of its heating. Cars run only on oil and industry uses mainly oil. Indeed, 78 per cent of all energy consumed in Quebec comes from oil. Some 200,000 barrels of oil enter Quebec every day from foreign countries; 300,000 come from the producing provinces in western Canada.
Is the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources at least concerned with making sure the supplies coming from within this country are assured, as he is certainly not able to assure the supplies from outside countries? No, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources aggravates the dialogue between Ottawa and the producing provinces. At the same time, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) laughs at the complaints of the producing provinces which want to obtain maximum protection for their resources and thus assure the economic welfare of their people. Those gentlemen who are supposed to be representing the interests of Canadians and Quebeckers so passionately are insulting the oil producing provinces of western Canada that must nevertheless heat Quebec homes this winter and enable Quebeckers to go to work.
During the last election, Mr. Speaker, Quebeckers who were convinced by the Liberals in Ottawa that to pay 18 cents more a gallon for their oil was a useless sacrifice will not have any oil for their cars no matter what price they are willing to pay.

In the meantime, the same Quebeckers that were convinced to reject an 18-cent increase, a small short-term sacrifice required to ensure Quebec's and Canada's economic future, achieve self-sufficiency and guarantee oil supplies to Quebec, these same Quebeckers have just gone through the 15-cent increase since February 18, 1980. Moreover, the former finance minister's budget that Liberals used as an excuse to defeat the Clark government also proposed to give Quebec families tax credits to offset all price increases. Right now this Liberal government is increasing oil prices 15 cents, without any tax credit.
In April, 1980, each Quebec family with revenues below $21,000 would have received a $15 per child and $40 per adult tax credit, with $30 per child and $80 per adult in 1981. So the average Quebec family would have received in 1981 a $220 tax credit, whether they paid taxes or not. Since that time Quebeckers saved 3 cents per gallon with the 15-cent increase for which they are receiving no tax credit, which they had to pay without hope of recovering it. They had to absorb the total increase needed without any compensation based on their revenue, low or otherwise. All paid equally, and the increase does not apply only to all but heating fuel. Our excise tax did not apply to heating fuel.
In the meantime, Liberals in Ottawa promised not to increase the cost of oil as much as Progressive Conservatives were proposing in order to ensure Quebeckers safe supplies of oil and develop Canadian wells to replace foreign ones. We were proposing a $4 increase for 1980 and a $4.50 one for 1981 and 1982. Until now, without the benefits of our integrated program that would have led to self-sufficiency in 1990, Liberals here in Ottawa would have allowed a $3 per barrel direct and indirect increase, but the price is now $4 more per barrel. In the meantime, the cost of subsidies we are paying on foreign oil is increasing tremendously.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, because you are indicating that my time is coming to an end, Quebeckers will have saved 3 cents to find themselves confronted with the danger of losing the free use of their cars if foreign oil becomes scarce. Mr. Speaker, the oil matter is basic in Quebec as elsewhere. The essential supply of oil must be ensured until Quebec can partially rely on its alternative regional resources.
We are aware of the importance of the debate. I deplore the fact that we have been discussing this matter for ten years. I cannot accept that the government should give, or try to give, the impression that it has found a new formula. Today, the blame lies with the fact that this government has been in power too long. It has not had the foresight to give Canada the autonomy we all wish for on both sides of the House.
To my mind, it is our duty to remind them of their faults and failure with regard to that foresight, which has been sadly lacking in parliamentary debates. If they were to make proposals to achieve self-sufficiency by taking into account private enterprise, because here in Canada private enterprise is important, they could get some form of support. But it is our duty to call them to order when they do not offer any guarantees or enough aid to the underprivileged when the time comes to make proposals in energy matters.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased
Energy
that we have this opportunity today, an opposition day, to discuss energy questions. These questions will, of course, be before the House again very soon, in a matter of weeks, when the new energy policy of the government is set forth. I am sorry, however, that my neighbour to the south in Etobicoke, having introduced this motion and having made a number of broad generalizations about the energy policy of the government, is not in the House and apparently was unable to stay for this discussion, even in fact to hear the reply of the minister to his earlier statements.
Be that as it may, I would wish to point out to the hon. member who introduced the motion that Canada is, after all, an energy-rich country, having an abundance of resources, and that we are, indeed, a net exporter of energy. Certainly in that sense there is no energy crisis in Canada. For example, we had in 1978 an excess of exports over imports of almost $2 billion. The cost of imported oil was more than offset by our exports of natural gas alone. In all areas, except oil, Canada has today a surplus of energy: in natural gas, hydroelectric power, coal, and uranium for nuclear power. Indeed, we export natural gas and we are negotiating the export of additional coal. On current account, in other words, we export more energy than we buy.
The challenge to Canadians in a sense is a challenge of managing abundance. This is an enviable position in today's energy-scarce world.
The current problem, of course, is in respect of oil and not the other areas of energy that I have mentioned. In that specific area of oil, Canada was until fairly recently self-sufficient. In light of the then estimates, we were even an exporter of oil. Unfortunately, that self-sufficiency has temporarily disappeared, but certainly the potential is there, especially in the oil sands, the offshore and the Arctic regions. Unlike almost all other industrial countries, Canada has enormous potential and enormous opportunity in energy.
Conventional sources in Alberta are expected to decline, but vast reserves in our oil sands, offshore, and in Arctic regions promise Canadians once again self-sufficiency. When cheaply produced oil in Alberta was available so too was cheap offshore oil. With those two sources, Canadians were provided with ample oil resources. With the suddenness of OPEC price increases, however, Canada was faced with the challenge of rapidly developing its non-conventional sources, a challenge which involved costly and technologically novel methods.
The results are now beginning to show in the oil sands, in the vast gas reserves identified in the Arctic, and in the offshore reserves of oil and gas on the Atlantic coast. The gap between when we were and when we again shall be self-sufficient has required imports of oil for which we have had to pay increasing amounts. We have subsidized those imports to ensure a gradual increase in price and to ensure equality of costs for all Canadians across Canada. Today we are at a stage when we need to phase in yet higher oil prices in Canada-let no one be mistaken that there will be higher oil prices-to compensate for our import costs and to ensure that the necessary further development of our petroleum industry continues

October 14, 1980
Energy
unabated. There will be higher prices, but they will not be world prices. We are committed in this government to maintain a made-in-Canada price which will blend the lower cost of conventional oil, the much higher cost of non-conventional oil and the imported oil, the price over which we have no control.
On the question of non-conventional oil pricing, there can now be little disagreement in principle. The minister pointed out that the government has proposed a price of $38 a barrel, plus an inflator which will provide the necessary funds to ensure that the additional oil sands projects go ahead as planned without interruption.
On the question of conventional oil, we all agree that the price must increase. There has, however, been some disagreement about tying that Canadian price to world levels. It is not our intention to do so and we are committed to a policy which will maintain a made-in-Canada price.
We have had some discussion this afternoon about matters which might better be described as fiscal rather than energy policy. We have talked about the division of oil revenue among the producers, the provinces, and the national government. As the minister pointed out, in all other federal states the revenue accruing to the central government is much greater in proportion to total revenue than here in Canada. Quite obviously there is a need at the federal level for more revenue to meet our obligations in respect of redistribution through equalization payments. There is obviously a need for more national revenue to reduce and eventually eliminate the oil compensation import program, and there is a need to ensure that energy projects receive the essential stimulus of the national government.
In addition, while we recognize the need of industry for funds to develop non-conventional sources, we see that there are also real requirements to move quickly and substantially in the direction of greater Canadian participation in the petroleum industry.
During these past days we have been discussing the patria-tion of our constitution. We have yet, in my view, to patriate our economy, and one part of that goal will be achieved by our energy policy which aims directly at the question of greater Canadianization of the oil industry.
In introducing this motion the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) referred to possible supply problems and painted a rather gloomy picture of possible disruptions in the supply to Canadians of their essential oil requirements. I would remind the House of the success of this government in negotiating and completing arrangements for the import of new sources of oil from Mexico, the delivery of which I am pleased to say will commence very shortly.
In addition, in Canada today we have Canadian oil inventories of approximately 160 million barrels, and that amount is by no means negligible. Those reserves amount to about 90 days of oil consumption and over 1,000 days-three years-of our current net oil imports.
Nevertheless, the government is also committed to alternatives which will also assist Canadians in being assured that their offshore oil supplies will be adequate to meet all essential needs. We are, for example, currently considering alternatives for establishing an emergency oil inventory. I might point out that given Canada's relatively modest oil imports, this emergency inventory need not be too large. An emergency stock of from 15 million to 25 million barrels would provide from six months' to one year's protection from a loss of 10 per cent to 20 per cent of our current crude oil imports. Even with larger disruptions, this inventory would provide time to evaluate the situation and implement, if necessary, our emergency allocation procedures.
Also in connection with the possibility of emergency supplies, which the hon. member raised earlier, we have made significant progress in the preparation of contingency plans for the allocation of crude oil to refineries and petroleum products to wholesale consumers. Should an emergency become so severe that rationing became necessary, plans are available for that as well.
I might also add that in the international arena we have engaged, with other industrialized countries of the western would, in a third international test to appraise the procedures of the allocation of oil under the International Energy Agency. This may suggest further improvements which might, as necessary, be made to our present procedures.
The hon. member opposite also spoke this afternoon about conservation and renewable energy. I should like for a moment to turn to those two subjects as a further illustration of the ways in which this government has acted, is acting, and will act to provide Canadians with a new energy policy capable of providing the security and fairness of supply which all Canadians have a right to seek.
In the context of energy conservation, the Government of Canada has recently moved, with the provincial governments, in co-operative programs intended to develop promising energy savings or alternative energy technologies. Most recently, an agreement was signed with the government of Saskatchewan. In total almost $120 million has been allocated for joint projects with provinces under this promising conservation program.
Industry is one of the major consumers of oil in Canada. We have worked out co-operative programs with various industry sectors, which has led to substantial savings already in the amount of oil they use, particularly in the manufacturing sector. In co-operation with industry, we have engaged in setting new targets which look for a 23 per cent reduction in the amount of oil consumed by Canadian industry over the base year 1975.
I hardly need remind the House-in any discussion of conservation-of the success of the Canadian Home Insulation Program. CHIP has made more than $200 million available to Canadians for more energy-efficient homes. As has already been announced, new arrangements and additions are being made to that program to ensure greater efficiency and further extension.
October 14, 1980

On the question of alternative sources, I was pleased that the hon. member opposite raised some questions in his opening statement because the record of the government in this area has been one of constant improvement since the first efforts in, for example, the solar area in 1978. The House may recall that at that time government funding of almost $400 million was offered to assist new research and development in renewable energies, particularly solar. Those programs have already begun to show results, although solar technology is not yet at a stage where it can be widely applied in oil saving procedures. There is no question in my mind that, while not looking for dramatic immediate pay-offs, we must make such investment in what is a Canadian industry offering real potential for the future.
More recently, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) announced further expansion of the federal programs intended to develop solar technology in Canada, including a program which will provide for the construction of a number of dwellings heated in part or in whole by solar water heaters.
In this area of solar energy, as indeed in the areas of a number of other renewable energy resources such as wind, tide or biomass, we are still at an early stage of technological development, but with the significant funding which is becoming available through the federal government in support of these programs I have no doubt of their ultimate success.
1 might say in addition that we on this side of the House welcome the recent announcements of the Ontario government regarding its commitment of substantial new funds toward the same end of promoting renewable energy sources in Canada.
1 might also note that the government announced in the Speech from the Throne the creation of a renewable energy corporation. That Crown corporation has a mandate to provide essential support for the promotion of renewable energy technologies beyond the demonstration stage and particularly to benefit smaller Canadian companies. The new corporation is now on its way to inception. Funding has been provided for its initial activities, and Petro-Canada is providing, for the moment, necessary administrative support while the new corporation comes into being.
With these few comments on our energy wealth and potential, and with one or two remarks about policies to ensure all Canadians adequate supplies of energy sources, I hope that 1 have indicated the government's general policy approach to the provision of energy in Canada. 1 hope, too, that by referring to the conservation initiatives and the new programs in renewable energy 1 have given substance to our commitment to the need as well to act on the demand side of the equation. In our view, it is not adequate simply to search for new sources of conventional energy within Canada. It is also essential that Canadians recognize and develop methods for conservation and for renewable sources.
With these references to the government's energy policy principles and objectives, to the evidence of the dynamic growth of our energy economy and to the many initiatives we have taken in the past six months, I trust that the House will
Energy
recognize that our management of Canada's energy situation is fully in accordance with our best national interests. The actions we have taken as a government have greatly reduced the threat to our national energy security experienced in the not too distant past. We will be announcing in the very near future new energy initiatives on the basis of the planning and decisions of the past six months which in our view will enable Canadians to meet the very serious challenges of energy supply and price, the problems of price impact on inflation and on the economy generally facing all countries in 1980. But I believe we in Canada have the opportunity to meet those challenges in a way that is unsurpassed by any other industrialized country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to participate in the debate on the motion moved by the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson). In order to refresh the minds of hon. members as to what we are debating on this allotted day, it is an opposition procedure by which the opposition can pick a subject and in effect debate the merits and demerits of that subject; it is sort of a replacement of the old supply procedure. But for those people in the television audience, this is one of the few opportunities the opposition has to bring to the fore issues which can be debated because it feels they carry a rather high priority.
Earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre ably led off the debate by moving the following motion:
That this House condemns the government for its mismanagement of Canada's energy situation with the consequent loss of economic development opportunities and increased threat to the nation's energy security.
Other than perhaps what is going on in Toronto today where the premiers are talking about the constitution, and what will take place tomorrow when the House recommences the debate on that topic, I do not believe there is a more fundamental question which affects the unity of this country than the question of energy and the policy, or the lack of one, from the federal government. When the scales are weighed up yonder, regardless of what happens to the Constitution of Canada and/or its reform and renewed federalism, there is no doubt in my mind that the policy or lack of policy of the present government on energy will be its single most important substantive indictment. Frankly, that covers a fantastic field because there are many other areas about which we can talk in which the government has not moved with much decision or knowledge. Naturally we in the opposition would think that.
I have only a brief remark to make about the comments of the hon. parliamentary secretary. I was a little disappointed that he reflected on the absence of the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre who moved this motion, it is nevertheless the minister's responsibility to be in the House and participate in the debate. He has a responsibility to the Canadian taxpayer and those who cannot pay taxes because they do not have enough money-there are almost more of those than taxpayers. If the minister has developed the arrogance of which many

October 14, 1980
Energy
have quite rightly accused him, if he can speak and then disappear, he has almost reversed what Caesar said when he came to Gaul. He would say, "I saw, I conquered and I left".
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) condescended to sit here and listen to the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre move the motion. He listened to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), the energy critic of the NDP, when he spoke. Perhaps he has good reasons in his mind for not being here today to discuss this fundamental issue of energy, but it is most unfair for the parliamentary secretary to the minister to stand in his place and comment on the absence of a member of the opposition who does not hold a ministerial post and is not paid an extra stipend by the Crown to discharge government business. I have another comment to make about the remarks of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. MacLaren). Again it is just a brief reference to Toronto. It is not just facts and figures or the writ of a constitution that makes constitutions or countries. It is an atmosphere; it is really a feeling which goes a long way toward getting into the intangibles of a constitution. But it is easy to understand why we have problems with the constitution and/or an energy package when we hear the minister of energy or his parliamentary secretary stand in the House and say that there is no crisis in energy. That was the purport of the minister's remarks earlier-that there is no crisis in energy. Mr. Speaker, I do not know where one would have to go in the western world today to find a country which does not have an energy crisis, unless one finds the foxhole Alice in Wonderland slid down years ago in that famous little book Lewis Carroll wrote, which I think the minister and the parliamentary secretary must have read, and lives in a fool's world. There is not a spokesman worthy of his salt who does not appreciate that every western country is confronted with an energy crisis regardless of how one might want to particularize. We talk about the export of gas and the parliamentary secretary says we are only a little short of oil. The parliamentary secretary only has to go east. He can go through the province of Quebec and certainly to Atlantic Canada, and when he is talking about a little deficiency in the supply of oil, he is talking about 80 per cent of the generation of energy in Nova Scotia and more than that in Prince Edward Island. That is real cause for concern in the minds of those in Atlantic Canada and, I would think, among many people in Quebec. It is the basis for what any moderate person would say is a crisis in energy. Whether one wants to talk about conventional sources, gas, solar, alternative supply or conservation, there is not a responsible person in the western world who does not realize that this is a problem on which we do not have a handle because the supply in so many cases is beyond our shores. As was intimated by the parliamentary secretary, the sad thing is that we have the potential, if developed, of developing a sufficiency of supply, and the previous government tried to do something about that. There is an honest difference of opinion. This was expressed in the vote last year and certainly it was expressed in the vote in February by the people of Canada.
Perhaps, with respect, they did not understand the full implications of what was attempted in the budget of December last year. The hon. member for Etobicoke Centre had to go to Toronto on parliamentary business. I think it is the height of hyprocrisy for the parliamentary secretary to comment about his absence when the minister responsible for the whole energy field is not in his place and perhaps we will not see him again for the rest of the day.
The minister made an allusion to Thanksgiving and offered some rejoinder as he started. When I heard his remarks, I thought he might have been speaking on April Fools' Day, poking fun, making jests and April Fools' jokes along with some of his larger generalizations. The minister can be a likeable person away from the House. I do not intend this personally, but in the discharge of his ministerial responsibilities, whether in the House or talking to fellow ministers in the provinces, this minister has a capacity to give a turkey indigestion when he tries to explain the problems in the energy field. Looking ahead in the holiday field-and again this is not a personal reflection-in the discharge of his duties outside the House he is a very affable and most humble man who has much about which to be humble; but in the House and dealing with his fellow counterparts in the provinces he has the capacity to make Santa Claus on Christmas Day into Scrooge. Instead of using his energy to develop the policies or the security of supply about which he talks, I submit he is creating discord and division across the land as great as any we have ever known outside Quebec in terms of our future and in terms of the constitution.
Worse than that, there is an element of deception in almost everything he says. I say this with reluctance because I do not want to deliberately accuse a minister of deceiving the House, but this is what is going on, whether it is intentional or unintentional and, frankly, the minister has more brains than a lot of people give him credit for. I do not believe it is unintentional. I believe it is very intentional and we saw several examples of it here today. All right, it can be a matter of debate for him taking pride in so many more wells being drilled this year but the minister knows that in order to drill a well this year you have to plan for it the year before. The real test of this government's mandate will be how many wells are drilled next year. If there is not a satisfactory oil pricing agreement I would venture to say-and I am prepared to bet the minister when he returns to the House-that there will not be as many wells drilled next year as this year if there is not an oil pricing agreement, and we have not seen one yet.
The parliamentary secretary commented on figures and the minister used figures. We all know-government members know, opposition members know and I think the public out there in televisionland know-that any politician worth his salt can play with figures. Figures lie or liars figure, but figures do not lie. Take the precise example the minister used in terms of deception-and I am not talking about the television ads across this land which are trying to lull Canadians into a false sense of complacency that we have security of supply-that we
October 14, 1980

have all those great reserves and resources out there. Getting around to developing them may be another question but do not worry too much. When you see that type of ad how interested are you going to be in conservation? I know what my children think when they see that ad. They ask me: Dad, don't we have a problem with oil in Atlantic Canada? I have to say yes. They ask: Then what is that ad telling us that everything is all right?
You can talk about all your programs-and the insulation program is good as far as it goes-but there have been some other projects involving alternative energy. 1 think of the Fundy tidal project which used to be in my riding and is now in the riding of the hon. member for Southwest Nova (Miss Campbell). That was an experimental project involving some $42 million, $25 million of which might be the forerunner of the development of tidal power in Canada. Certainly, in Atlantic Canada that could be an alternative source of energy.
But where is the incentive to develop those alternate sources or follow any conservation program in our daily life when there are ads on television which say it is all right, don't worry, Canada is the greatest and there is lots of potential under the ground and under the sea? The exercise defeats its own purpose, Mr. Speaker.
But let us look at the figures used by the minister today. He talked about Texas. I am not the expert in terms of figures but 1 have these from a fundamental source. The very fraction that he talked about he compared to Texas. He was talking about Alberta. This deception is repeated and repeated so that people think that Alberta is the only bad boy in this picture. The minister knows, even if the parliamentary secretary does not, that it is not 45 per cent that goes to Alberta from the first dollar to the last dollar. The hon. gentleman over there smiles and 1 take it the smile is in acquiescence. He does know it is a weighted figure. I have heard 45 per cent at federal-provincial conferences, I have heard it on radio, 1 have heard commentators use it and until I heard the minister use it again today and then went behind the curtains to talk to a couple of members who are more knowledgeable in this field than I am, I did not fully appreciate how deceptive that figure is. The 45 per cent that Alberta supposedly gets is a weighted figure. The province does not get 45 per cent of every dollar that flows into their coffers. Of the first four dollars they only get 16'/2 per cent. And the figure is weighted up to the 45 per cent. The average, Mr. Speaker, is 37 per cent.
What does that 37 per cent do on $16-a-barrel oil in Alberta? Let us not talk about paying the Mexicans $34 or $36 a barrel. That money would go out of the country and would not develop a thing in Canada. Let us just talk about the $16-less than half the world price-that we pay our fellow Canadians. Thirty-seven per cent of the $16 works out to $5.92 a barrel. The 17 per cent that the minister says is paid to the Texan state government, because they are getting much more as their wholesale price, works out to $6.46. If my figures are wrong I hope the minister will stand in this House tomorrow and ask me to correct this calculation. 1 have it from a man in our opposition who knows much more about oil than I do and I take his figures as being correct. I saw the charts
Energy
behind them. But, Mr. Speaker, I am willing to stand and be the one to be rebuked if I am in error. This is just an example which, on my information, shows the deception in regard to this whole energy picture. I find it a very interesting situation when the minister relies on the Texas reed and realizes it is a broken reed, a broken straw.
There are so many other things one could say in the brief time allotted. The minister said he was going to talk about three points. I hope he will start by talking to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). In that memorable speech which the then leader of the opposition, now the Prime Minister, gave during the election campaign before the Board of Trade in Halifax on January 25, the Prime Minister did not talk about three commitments, he talked about seven major commitments. There were seven major commitments and I am going to talk about one, the Q and M pipeline. Only two have even come close to being acknowledged. Let us take the minister's words. Forget about the Prime Minister who made seven commitments only two of which have even been acknowledged, and let us take the three the hon. gentleman mentioned here today. He talked about security of supply, alternatives and conservation.
I won't repeat some of what I have said but in terms of supply we have not got an oil pricing agreement, we have not got the development of the tar sands and our supply picture is questionable. Wayne Cheveldayoff, in an article he wrote for The Globe and Mail on May 12, 1980, before he became assistant to the governor of the Bank of Canada-and I think everyone in this House and certainly members opposite would agree with me that Wayne Cheveldayoff would be a very objective commentator on the energy scene-said that within six years the conventional supply, in effect from Alberta, will be used up unless we develop some of those frontier supplies. We are talking about Canadianizing the oil industry. If we do not get down to developing our oil industry, Mr. Speaker, we will have no oil industry to Canadianize.
The minister's second point was fairness between regions. 1 want to ask the parliamentary secretary how fair is it to end the Q and M pipeline in Quebec and not extend it to Atlantic Canada, though the Prime Minister promised he would do so in the campaign; the Liberal party in a full page ad after the Prime Minister spoke in Halifax promised, in point three, that there would be a natural gas pipeline to ensure all Canadians access to their resources. It said:
Liberals would take immediate action to begin negotiations for construction of a natural gas pipeline to Quebec City and the maritimes.
To quote the Prime Minister's words which appear on page ten of his speech-it was one of the few printed speeches in the campaign:
I am announcing today, as part of our program, that a Liberal government will take immediate action to ensure the full co-operation of all parties in the construction of a natural gas pipeline to Quebec City and the maritimes.
Mr. Speaker, the cabinet can either accept or reject a National Energy Board decision. I charge the Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen), the two ministers from Nova Scotia in this minis-

October 14, 1980
Energy
try-and I do not know who else is from Atlantic Canada because we do not hear about them down there-with selling out the interests of Atlantic Canada by not rejecting the NEB report.
The NEB says that the need for environmental studies is the reason we should not proceed. They know and the minister knows that gas pipelines, and there are all sorts of them buried across this country with grass growing on top of them, would follow the hydro lines which are a worse environmental eyesore. The fuel being transported is gas, which is a heck of a lot less polluting than coal. If there were a break in the pipeline or any other problem, we would know, as he knows and they should know, that in terms of environmental impact the blow-off of methane is a heck of a lot less harmful than many other spills.
They tried to justify not extending the Q and M pipeline by saying there might be something offshore in Sable. We in Atlantic Canada know, as the minister and the NEB should know, that any development offshore would be within a three-year to four-year range which would coincide with the building or construction of a pipeline beyond Quebec if it got under way today. The environmental studies are merely an excuse for the minister. I believe the NEB did a disservice to Atlantic Canada, but it is supposedly beyond parliamentary criticism. I am starting to wonder if it should be.
The whole matter is a political question for the same reason as the building of the CPR to the west to tie it in with the rest of Canada back in 1867 was a political question. It should be a political decision made by a government with fibre in its soul and an interest in all of Canada, not just pieces of Canada, to make sure that that pipeline goes from coast to coast and certainly beyond Quebec into Atlantic Canada.
I cannot get very excited over what the minister said today about fairness to the regions. He need not talk to me about fairness to regions. I am sure there are members on the other side from the province of Newfoundland who must be embarrassed at the present position of the federal government in not allowing the government of Newfoundland to transmit power across Quebec from Churchill Falls. What is the rationale? How can there be a double standard, letting pipelines cross provinces yet not allowing a hydro line to cross Quebec?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENTAL MISMANAGEMENT OF ENERGY SITUATION
speechtext:
In conclusion, because I know my time is just about up, I will talk about offshore rights which the present government will not honour. I would like to draw attention to an article in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of October 4 which deals not only with the offshore problem today but with some of the history of this country and points out facts which make our offshore situation even more accute and compounds the sense of unfairness which we in Atlantic Canada feel.
As other provinces came into confederation, be it Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta or Quebec, vast territories in the north were given to them by act of this Parliament. We do not begrudge this. But, for example, one of the most important developments in Quebec, the James Bay project, is located in this territory. Much of the development which took place in Alberta and Saskatchewan is found in such northern areas. The size of these territories is immense, with approximately 379,000 square miles going to Quebec, approximately 382,000 square miles to Ontario and approximately 237,000 miles to Manitoba. Alberta and Saskatchewan each received 250,000 square miles of new territory.
If one turns to Nova Scotia, which has only 20,000 square miles of territory in total, one can begin to appreciate why in the deep east, if we have any feeling for the deep east and are true sons of the deep east, we feel there is a double standard. We do not mind other provinces getting the territories which make up their present boundaries because it has obviously helped us with regard to equalization grants.
What we cannot understand is why there is not some recognition of the mineral wealth off our shores since those other provinces, through those extra gifts of land, received so much wealth. I would hope the minister will come back into the House and address his mind to a couple of the matters which I have raised.
The most interesting and ironic situation came up when the minister talked about the third item.
I have a different clock from yours, Mr. Speaker, but since yours is the one that governs us, I gather you are indicating that my time is up. In conclusion, the third item mentioned by the minister had to do with Canadian participation in the oil industry. There are reliable assessments that, based on the known supply in this country at the present time, we will not have any oil within a ten-year period unless we develop non-conventional resources. The interesting thing which the minister did not tell us is that it was the fledgling oil industry in the west, when Turner Valley was first discovered during the 1940s, which came east to look for financing. That industry came to the Government of Canada of the day for financing. It happened to be the same type of government in power, a Liberal government, as is the case now, and has, unfortunately, been the case for so long.
Because of the lack of financing from eastern financiers and the government, the oil industry had to go south of the border for financing to develop its fantastic oil potential. I hope that some of the deception, discord and division which is constantly being sown by the minister on this issue will be directed to resolving problems rather than to creating more problems.
